excerpt: Trapped in the Philippines after the fall of Cañacao, eleven U.S. Navy nurses spent over three years maintaining care under siege and internment. The story of Dorothy Still Danner records their discipline, tactical foresight, and eventual rescue at Los Baños.
author: Lexi Zotomayor
imageAlt: Dorothy Still and Eldene Paige comfort an internee who had fainted following their rescue rom the Los Banos camp. Photo taken by Carl Mydans
bodyText:
In late 1941, Cañacao Naval Hospital occupied a narrow peninsula in Cavite, bounded by the main Navy Yard and the seaplane ramps at Sangley Point. Banyan trees shaded the stone arcades, and amber lights glowed along the seawall after dusk. Routine governed daily life: Mondays brought post-liberty medical reviews, Wednesdays required preparation for Thursday's full-dress inspection, and Fridays cleared the administrative desk for the weekend.

Dorothy Still had arrived in the Philippines aboard the transport ship USS *Henderson* in 1939. Working alongside ten other U.S. Navy nurses under Chief Nurse Laura Cobb, she managed wards filled with sailors, military dependents, and civilian yard workers. War was expanding across Western Europe and China, but inside the Cavite naval enclave,hospital operations ran on schedule.

The routine ended on December 10, 1941.

At noon, Japanese high-altitude bombers struck Manila Bay. In forty-five minutes, the Navy Yard and hospital complex were reduced to rubble. Power failed instantly. Water mains burst. Secondary explosions from nearby ammunition dumps shook the remaining concrete foundations. Casualties arrived at the triage desks continuously—sailors,civilians, and construction crews.

Standard admission protocols collapsed. Medical staff made immediate decisions at the door. Recalling the incoming surge, Dorothy noted:

> *"Triage was impossible. You just tried to find out which were the worst ones to go to surgery..."*

Working without clean linen, running water, or rest, Dorothy and her colleagues began emergency surgical prep.Cañacao was destroyed. No orders for evacuation arrived from headquarters. The nurses stayed at their posts.

### Evacuation to Manila

Remaining inside the Cavite Navy Yard grew impossible within hours. Fires burned unchecked, and the risk of further air attacks forced the medical staff to move surviving patients across Manila Bay to Sternberg General Hospital, the U.S. Army's central facility in the capital.

Transporting the wounded across damaged roads required constant improvisation. Ammunition trucks, private cars, and converted delivery vans carried casualties through smoke and debris into Manila. Nurses stayed in the cargo beds during transit to manage hemorrhage control and secure field dressings.

Sternberg was already operating beyond capacity upon their arrival. Stretchers filled every hallway. As Japanese forces advanced through northern Luzon, military authorities declared Manila an open city to prevent urban bombardment.Medical units received orders to consolidate and convert civilian schools into temporary hospital space.

The Navy unit moved their wards again, occupying the campus of Santa Scholastica’s College. Classrooms and assembly halls were converted into patient wards over a single night.

Chief Nurse Laura Cobb immediately secured their medical inventory. Knowing that advancing forces would confiscate military pharmaceuticals, Cobb directed the nurses to strip commercial labels from essential drug supplies.Bottled supplies of quinine and anti-malarial compounds were transferred into generic containers marked with common chemical names.

The strategy kept the supply intact. When Japanese forces inspected the building weeks later, the anti-malarial inventory remained on the shelves, unrecorded and unconfiscated.

### Internment at Santo Tomas

Japanese troops occupied Manila on January 2, 1942. On January 7, military officers entered Santa Scholastica, placed the eleven Navy nurses under arrest, and transferred them to the newly established internment camp at Santo Tomas University.

The university compound held nearly four thousand civilian internees behind fenced gates. Dormitories designed for small student cohorts were packed with hundreds of bunks placed edge to edge.

The nurses adapted their duty schedules to civilian internment. Chief Nurse Cobb established daily shifts in the makeshift camp clinic to treat dysentery, dengue fever, and early-stage malnutrition. The relabeled quinine supply preserved at Santa Scholastica prevented malaria from spreading through the overcrowded dormitories during the first year of confinement.

Camp life settled into an enforced daily pattern: morning and evening roll calls, mandatory bows to perimeter guards,and steadily shrinking food rations. Despite the loss of military status, the nurses wore their whites on shift,maintaining clinical standards inside the infirmary while waiting for news from the front.

### Transfer to Los Baños

By mid-1943, severe overcrowding at Santo Tomas forced the camp administration to build a satellite facility forty miles south at an agricultural college in Los Baños, situated at the base of Mount Makiling.

Chief Nurse Cobb, working with internee physician Dr. Charles Leach, requested that the Navy nurses be included in the early transfers to the new site. The unbuilt camp lacked basic sanitation infrastructure, and early labor details faced immediate risks from tropical disease and exhaustion.

The transfer order came in May 1944. The eleven nurses were moved south by rail alongside several hundred internees.

The journey took place in sealed, unventilated boxcars along the Manila Railroad line. At Los Baños, the concrete buildings of Santo Tomas were replaced by open wooden barracks with thatched roofs and dirt floors.

Rations decreased rapidly through late 1944. Daily meals were reduced to small portions of unhusked rice and cassava,supplemented by edible wild greens pulled from the perimeter fence line. Beriberi, pellagra, and extreme weight loss became standard conditions across the barracks.

The nurses kept the infirmary operational despite their own physical decline. They washed and boiled bandages for reuse, treated tropical ulcers with weak antiseptic solutions, and recorded vital signs daily.

### The Raid of February 23, 1945

By February 1945, camp food reserves were nearly exhausted. On the night of February 22, Dorothy was managing the overnight shift in the infirmary ward.

> *"I was on duty that night. There was a newborn baby and I was trying to feed her with what little powdered milk was left. The mother could hardly nurse the baby. She hadn't had enough nourishment herself..."*

At dawn on February 23, 1945, elements of the U.S. Army's 11th Airborne Division dropped by parachute directly over the camp perimeter, coordinating with local Filipino guerrilla units already surrounding the guard posts. As perimeter fire ceased, tracked amphibious vehicles broke through the outer fence lines.

Dorothy recalled the arrival of the rescue unit:

> *"An amtrac pulled up in front of the hospital and American troops jumped out. We never saw anything so handsome in our lives. These fellows looked so healthy and so lively... This whole thing went off with just the most amazing precision that you could imagine."*

All eleven Navy nurses and more than two thousand civilian internees were loaded into amphibious tractors, driven to the shores of Laguna de Bay, and transported across the water to Allied lines.
